latin.145: Tranfit ille Vir doctus ad vers. XIX. Ex eoque sic argumentatur. Constituti sumus peccatores per inobedientiam Adami; Ergo nobis imputata fuit. Mediante corruptione hereditaria, Concedo: Immediate, Nego. Videtur probare velle consequentiam. Nam qui quaeso, inquit, illa κατάστασις, illa ἁμαρτία, illud παράπτωμα, nos potuit reos constituere, τὸ παράπτωμα Rom. vers. 18. (quod quidem est actus judiciarius, justitiae Dei effatum, & effectum, damnatio, condemnatio) in nos inducere citra peccatum actuale, vel proprium, vel imputatum? Apage hoc delirium. Facilis est responsio. Potest nos reos constituere, ut loquitur Chamierus, causaliter, producto & propagato in nos peccato originali. Neque id est delirium; sed constans Ecclesiae doctrina, quam veram esse Scriptura & experientia contestantur. Quomodo, subjungit, constitui peccatores, scilicet actu, sine peccato? Quod cum non possit esse originale, quippe quod tantum adhuc habituale, praesertim in recens conceptis aut natis, superest ut sit quoddam actuale peccatum. Respondeo, constitui peccatores non sine peccato: nam peccatum originale est vere peccatum. At non est actu. Imo est actu peccatum habituale: actu inhaeret infantibus: actu nos facit reos irae divinae. Hoc si negas, a Pighii opinione vix distas.
latin.146: Suggillat etiam nostram responsionem, In re sitam esse similitudinem oppositionis, non in rei modo; ac dicit nos Socini potius quam Calvini partes tueri: cum tamen ipse revera discedat a Calvino, cui nos arcte adhaeremus. Quomodo autem illam responsionem, quam supra & autoritate & ratione comprobavimus, refutat? petit, cur ergo nostrates justificationis nostrae modum, nempe per imputationem justitiae Christi hinc eliciunt? Haec est scilicet egregia refutandi ratio! Quinam vero sunt illi nostrates qui id hinc eliciunt? Calvinus? Martyr? Bucerus? Bullingerus &c? Nequaquam certe; sed recentiores, ab eorum vestigiis ea in re deflectentes. At, inquit, non vident quantum communem causam laedant, qui hoc sibi invictum argumentum non solum eripi patiuntur, sed & nobis, ut adversae causae faveant, quantum in eis situm est, eripiunt. Et si cur hunc locum ita luxent, anquiramus; id in gratiam Pelagianorum, Arminianorum, Socinianorum, Anabaptistarum fieri certo comperiemus. Imo vero videmus quantum causam communem laedant, qui bene argumentari, vel nesciunt vel nolunt, argumentaque nullius roboris pro invictis obtrudunt, & interim fratres suos calumniis obruunt. Hoc certe & videmus & dolemus.
latin.147: Caetera praetermitto, nudas sine ratione affirmationes: illud tantum subiungam, quod & speciem aliquam prae se fert argumenti, & quam a publica fidei nostrae Confessione recedant & ad Pighianismum accedant illi qui nos accusant, prodit. Si peccatum, inquit, primi parentis non imputatur, quid opus imputatione meritorum Christi? Si vel peccatum originale intelligeret, vel imputationem mediatam, nihil diceret causae, quam agimus repugnans, diceret tantum aliquid falsum, & Theologo indignum, ne dicam Christiano. Opus enim nobis est imputatione justitiae Christi, ut etiam ab aliis peccatis nostris, quae nimium multa sunt, justificemur: Sed cum peccatum actuale Adami intelligat, illiusque imputationem immediatam, quis non videt ab eo peccati originalis reatum negari? Idque peccatum, quantum ad condemnationem vel justificationem attinet, pro nullo haberi? Sufficit, addit, sanctificatio quae tollat illum morbum. Est-ne igitur, inquam, ita morbus ut non sit peccatum? ut non damnet? Confer quaeso cum hujusmodi hominum doctrina articulum XI. Confessionis fidei; Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet, quamvis qui filii Dei sunt, minime idcirco condemnentur, quoniam videlicet Deus pro gratuita sua bonitate & misericordia illud ipsis non imputat. Dicimus praeterea hanc perversitatem semper edere fructus aliquos malitiae & rebellionis, &c.
latin.148: Vides hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, omnes homines aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragere, nisi condonetur, imputari, & negabis nobis opus esse imputatione meritorum Christi ut justificemur ab hoc vitio? Ita qui nobis in hac causa adversantur ejus culpae rei sunt, cujus nos falso accusant: discedunt enim a recepta doctrina. Quod ergo addit, O sic tota illa nostrae justificationis evangelicae doctrina, quam eximia, quam admiranda! ex horum φρονημάτων aut corruet tota, aut saltem inutilis reddetur; cernis, ut opinor, Lector, quam falsum & calumniosum sit. Idem accidit Clarissimo viro D. Steph. Blanco, cujus Disputatio Theologica de animae humanae origine, & modo quo propagatur peccatum originale prodiit in lucem eodem anno 1648. Is enim Th. XLII. sic disputat. Omnes peccaverunt peccato scilicet illo, quod per unum hominem introiit in mundum; at non peccaverunt peccato illo in sua persona, quia non extiterunt. Ergo peccaverunt in Adamo, quippe in quo mortui sunt I. Cor. 15. 22. Quanquam enim admitti posset conclusio, si recte intelligeretur; tamen minor propositio nihil aliud esse videtur, quam eius negatio, quod articulo illo XI. ab Ecclesiis nostris asseritur. Negat enim vitium illud esse peccatum quod per unum hominem in mundum, id est, in omnes homines introiit, quod tamen vitium in illo articulo & vere peccatum esse, & omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragere dicitur; quod efficere non posset, nisi in omnes & singulos homines introiisset.
latin.149: Quod etiam subiungit, quippe in quo mortui sunt, confirmat nostram sententiam: non enim cum in Adamo mori omnes dicuntur, mors ipsius Adami intelligitur, una numero, omnibus imputata; sed mors secundum hominum numerum multiplicata, ac sua cuique propria. Addit, & mortui unius illius hominis offensa Rom. 5. 15. unde, inquit, promptum est colligere, illam offensam fuisse omnium offensam, puta imputatione: repugnat enim justitiae divinae ut quis alienae poenae sit particeps, & non sit ullo modo particeps culpae. Si quis similiter diceret, nos fuisse productos unius illius hominis operatione vel virtute, num inde sequeretur, illam operationem vel virtutem fuisse omnium communem imputatione? Si repugnat justitiae divinae, ut quis alienae poenae sit particeps, & non sit ullo modo particeps culpae, certe eidem etiam justitiae repugnat, ut fiat particeps culpae judicis imputatione, is, qui alioqui non esset culpae particeps. Si judex facit injuste ei poenam irrogans, qui nullo modo est particeps culpae, quanto major erit injustitia, si non modo poenam irroget, sed eum faciat etiam sua actione & judiciaria imputatione participem culpae, atque adeo peccatorem & reum, alioqui non peccatorem nec reum? Miror hoc a viris piis & doctis non considerari. Quis enim innocens puniri juste non poterit, si facit imputatio commune esse peccatum quod alioqui non fuisset commune, & esse vere peccatorem & reum, qui alioqui peccator non fuisset?
latin.150: Tandem, ait vir doctus, vox illa ἁμαρτίαν in loco Paulino non significat habitum peccati, seu habitualem corruptionem, quae ipsis etiam infantibus inest, sed actum peccandi, eumque praeteritum, quo non potest intelligi aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Hoc vero est Calvino & aliis viris maximis, quos sequimur, contradicere, illud peccaverunt de vitio originali exponentibus. Affert tamen rationes. Quia I. inquit, loquitur Paulus de peccato quod introiit in mundum. i. in omnes homines, per Adamum, quem vocat unum hominem. Supponit vitium originale, aut non esse peccatum, aut non introiisse in omnes homines per unum illum hominem naturaliter procreatos. II. quia, hoc peccato involvuntur etiam infantes: sunt enim in censu hominum, & ex eorum numero, in quos mors transiit, nec moriuntur propter aliud peccatum actuale quam imputatum, quia aliud actuale in eos non cadit: actuale autem imputatum non est aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Non moriuntur quidem infantes propter aliud peccatum actuale quam primum illud Adami: sed cur non moriuntur proxime propter vitium illud habituale, quod omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragit? Hoc est quod jam non semel observavi, non posse imputationem immediatam primi Adae peccati actualis astrui, nisi negato habitualis vitii reatu. III. inquit, cum Paulus dicit vers. 17. mortem regnasse per unam offensam & vers. 19. multos esse constitutos peccatores unius hominis inobedientia; verba ista una offensa, & unius hominis inobedientia, non possunt aliud respicere quam ipsum factum Adami. i. divini mandati violationem. Esto, quid tum postea? Num inde sequitur, verbum ἁμαρτίαν non significare habitum peccati? aut primum Adami peccatum actuale nobis imputari immediate, seu prius quam nascamur corrupti? Mors regnat per unam offensam ita secundum habitum propagatam in omnes, ut in omnibus regnet mors, quia regnat peccatum. Unius hominis inobedientia secundum habitum propagata & multiplicata multi sunt constituti peccatores. Cur proximam mortis nostrae causam in alio quaerimus, cum se prodat ipsa in nobis, in corpore nostro, ac membris nostris, inhaerens, nempe illud peccatum, quod nisi crucifigatur gratia Christi, tam impotenter in nobis regnat?
latin.151: Subjungit th. XLIII. Mortem illam, quae per unum hominem in omnes homines pertransiit &c. includere suae significationis ambitu mortem spiritualem, seu animae, quae nihil aliud est, quam privatio justitiae originalis cum positione contrariae corruptionis habitualis &c: Hoc qua facilitate affirmatur, eadem negari potest; itaque probandum erat: quod vir doctus ne conatur quidem. De sola corporis & aeterna morte Confessio Helvetica, omnesque melioris notae interpretes mortem illam accipiunt, esseque accipiendam probabitur alio loco. Quod subiicit, sine imputatione inobedientiae Adami derivationem habitualis naturae humanae corruptionis non posse esse justam, id quomodo verum esse possit considerare oportet. Derivatio enim illa, cum sit aliud nihil quam contagium peccati & propagatio injustitiae, ipsa per se justa non est, nec esse potest. Non enim justum est propagare & multiplicare injustitiam. Sed illius derivationis permissio seu non impeditio divina justa est, nihilque habet justitiae repugnans. Quam adjungit rationem, Qua enim justitia & aequitate sustineremus omnes illius peccati poenam, nempe mortem spiritualem, si peccatum illud nobis non imputatur? Ea primum supponit, id quod inter nos controvertitur, vitium originale nobis a Deo infligi, & esse poenam proprie dictam. Deinde imputatio peccati alieni, qua nostrum fiat, non tollit injustitiam, sed auget potius: quasi Deus aequissimus & sanctissimus omnibus hominibus primum imputaret alienum peccatum, quo eos faceret imputative peccatores & reos, deinde ut illud imputatum puniret eos faceret inhaerenter peccatores. Ita unum tantum hominem Diabolus tentatione sua fecisset peccatorem, Deus sua actione, id est, imputatione, fecisset omnes homines peccatores & perditos. Quomodo fieri potest, ut pia conscientia tale dogma non detestetur? Nihil amplius argumenti apud hunc autorem reperio, quod non sit jam satis refutatum, ut nihil opus sit inani repetitione fastidio esse Lectori. Tantum, quod pene praeterieram, illud sine aliqua censura dimittendum non videtur, quod ait Th. XLI. Palam est, quicquid delinquat aliquis ut caput alicujus societatis, aut multitudinis, illud juste toti communitati imputari. Nam si id verum est, male omnino agebatur cum Romanis, cum eorum caput esset Nero aut Caligula: quippe quibus omnibus & singulis juste imputari poterat quicquid scelerati illi imperatores delinquebant: ita nullus erat in toto imperio Romano, qui non esset parricida, siquidem parricidium a capite commissum omnibus Romanis juste imputabatur.

pass_a.145: That learned man passes over to verse 19. And from it he argues thus. We were constituted sinners through Adam's disobedience; therefore it was imputed to us. By means of hereditary corruption, I grant; immediately, I deny. He seems to want to prove the consequence. For who, I ask, he says, could that κατάστασις, that ἁμαρτία, that παράπτωμα, constitute us guilty, [or] lead τὸ παράπτωμα of Rom. verse 18 (which indeed is a judicial act, an utterance of God's justice, and its effect—damnation, condemnation) into us apart from actual sin, whether proper or imputed? Away with this delirium. The reply is easy. It can constitute us guilty, as Chamier speaks, causally, by original sin produced and propagated into us. Nor is that delirium; but the Church's constant doctrine, which Scripture and experience attest to be true. How, he adds, be constituted sinners, namely in act, without sin? Which since it cannot be original—inasmuch as that is still only habitual, especially in the newly conceived or born—it remains that it is some actual sin. I answer: we are constituted sinners not without sin: for original sin is truly sin. But it is not [actual] in act. Rather it is in act a habitual sin: in act it inheres in infants: in act it makes us liable to divine wrath. If you deny this, you scarcely differ from Pighius's opinion.
pass_a.146: He also gibes at our reply, that the likeness of the opposition is seated in the thing, not in the mode of the thing; and he says we defend Socinus's side rather than Calvin's: when yet he himself in truth departs from Calvin, to whom we cling closely. But how does he refute that reply which above we proved both by authority and by reason? He asks, why then do our people draw from here the mode of our justification, namely through the imputation of Christ's righteousness? This, forsooth, is a splendid way of refuting! Who then are those of ours who draw it from here? Calvin? Martyr? Bucer? Bullinger, and so on? Certainly by no means; but more recent men, turning aside from their footsteps in that matter. But, he says, they do not see how much they wound the common cause, who not only allow this supposedly invincible argument to be snatched from themselves, but also, so far as in them lies, snatch it from us that they may favor the adverse cause. And if we inquire why they so luxuriate in this place, we shall certainly find it is done as a favor to Pelagians, Arminians, Socinians, Anabaptists. On the contrary, we see how much they wound the common cause who either do not know how or refuse to argue well, thrust forward arguments of no strength as invincible, and meanwhile overwhelm their brothers with calumnies. This certainly we both see and grieve over.
pass_a.147: The rest I pass by—bare affirmations without reason: I will only add this, which both wears some appearance of an argument and shows how far those who accuse us recede from our public Confession of faith and approach Pighianism. If, he says, the first parent's sin is not imputed, what need is there of the imputation of Christ's merits? If he meant either original sin or mediate imputation, he would say nothing contrary to the cause we plead; he would only say something false and unworthy of a theologian, not to say of a Christian. For we need the imputation of Christ's righteousness so that we may also be justified from our other sins, which are all too many: but when he means Adam's actual sin and its immediate imputation, who does not see that the guilt of original sin is denied by him? And that that sin, as far as condemnation or justification is concerned, is held for nothing? It is enough, he adds, [to have] sanctification which takes away that disease. Is it then, I ask, a disease such that it is not sin? such that it does not condemn? Compare, I beg, with such men's doctrine article XI of the Confession of faith: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes all and every human being—not even little ones still hiding in their mothers' wombs excepted—guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin as regards blame, although those who are sons of God are by no means therefore condemned, because God of his free goodness and mercy does not impute it to them. We say besides that this perversity always brings forth some fruits of malice and rebellion, and so on.
pass_a.148: You see that this vice is truly sin, that it makes all men guilty of eternal death before God unless it is forgiven—[that it] is imputed—and will you deny that we need the imputation of Christ's merits that we may be justified from this vice? So those who oppose us in this cause are guilty of the very fault of which they falsely accuse us: for they depart from the received doctrine. What he therefore adds—'O how excellent, how wonderful, that whole doctrine of our evangelical justification! from these φρονημάτα it will either wholly collapse, or at least be rendered useless'—you see, I think, Reader, how false and slanderous it is. The same happens to the most distinguished man D. Stephen Blancus, whose Theological Disputation on the origin of the human soul and the mode by which original sin is propagated came to light in the same year 1648. For in Thesis XLII he disputes thus. All sinned by that sin, namely, which entered the world through one man; but they did not sin by that sin in their own person, because they did not yet exist. Therefore they sinned in Adam, inasmuch as in him they died (1 Cor. 15:22). Although the conclusion could be admitted if rightly understood, yet the minor proposition seems to be nothing other than the denial of what is asserted in that article XI by our Churches. For he denies that that vice is the sin which entered the world—that is, into all men—through one man; yet in that article that vice is said both to be truly sin and to make all and every human being guilty of eternal death before God; which it could not effect unless it had entered into all and every human being.
pass_a.149: What he also adds—'inasmuch as in him they died'—confirms our view: for when all are said to die in Adam, Adam's own death is not understood as one in number, imputed to all; but death multiplied according to the number of men, and each one's own. He adds, and they died by the offense of that one man (Rom. 5:15); whence, he says, it is ready to gather that that offense was everyone's offense, namely by imputation: for it is contrary to divine justice that anyone should share another's punishment and not share the guilt in any way. If someone likewise said we were produced by that one man's operation or power, would it follow that that operation or power was common to all by imputation? If it is contrary to divine justice that anyone share another's punishment and not share guilt in any way, certainly it is also contrary to the same justice that one who otherwise would not share guilt should be made a sharer of guilt by the judge's imputation. If a judge acts unjustly in laying a penalty on one who in no way shares guilt, how much greater the injustice if he not only lays on the penalty but by his own act and judicial imputation also makes him a sharer of guilt—and so a sinner and guilty—who otherwise was neither sinner nor guilty? I marvel that pious and learned men do not consider this. For who that is innocent could not be justly punished, if imputation makes common a sin that otherwise would not have been common, and makes truly a sinner and guilty one who otherwise would not have been a sinner?
pass_a.150: At last, says the learned man, that word ἁμαρτίαν in the Pauline place does not signify the habit of sin, or the habitual corruption which is in infants themselves also, but the act of sinning, and that a past one, by which nothing else can be understood except Adam's first sin. But this is to contradict Calvin and the other greatest men whom we follow, who explain that 'they sinned' of original vice. Yet he brings reasons. Because, I., he says, Paul speaks of the sin which entered the world, that is, into all men, through Adam, whom he calls one man. He assumes that original vice either is not sin, or did not enter into all men naturally begotten through that one man. II. because infants also are involved in this sin: for they are in the census of men, and of their number into whom death passed, and they do not die because of any other actual sin than an imputed one, because no other actual [sin] falls on them: but an imputed actual [sin] is nothing other than Adam's first sin. Infants indeed do not die because of any other actual sin than that first of Adam: but why do they not die proximately because of that habitual vice which makes all and every human being guilty of eternal death before God? This is what I have more than once observed: immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin cannot be built up unless the guilt of the habitual vice is denied. III. he says, when Paul says in verse 17 that death reigned through one offense and in verse 19 that many were constituted sinners by one man's disobedience, those words 'one offense' and 'one man's disobedience' cannot look to anything but Adam's own deed, that is, the violation of the divine command. Be it so—what then? Does it follow that the word ἁμαρτίαν does not signify the habit of sin? or that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately, that is, before we are born corrupt? Death reigns through one offense so propagated according to habit into all that death reigns in all, because sin reigns. By one man's disobedience propagated and multiplied according to habit, many are constituted sinners. Why seek elsewhere the proximate cause of our death, when it betrays itself in us—in our body and members—inhering, namely that sin which, unless crucified by Christ's grace, reigns so mightily in us?
pass_a.151: He subjoins in Thesis XLIII that that death which passed through to all men through one man, etc., includes within the scope of its meaning spiritual death, or of the soul, which is nothing other than the privation of original righteousness with the positing of the contrary habitual corruption, etc. With the same ease this is affirmed, it can be denied; therefore it needed to be proved: which the learned man does not even attempt. Of bodily and eternal death alone the Helvetic Confession, and all interpreters of better note, take that death, and that it is to be so taken will be proved in another place. What he adds—that without imputation of Adam's disobedience the derivation of habitual corruption of human nature cannot be just—how that can be true must be considered. For that derivation, since it is nothing other than the contagion of sin and the propagation of injustice, is not itself just, nor can it be. For it is not just to propagate and multiply injustice. But the divine permission or non-hindering of that derivation is just, and has nothing contrary to justice. The reason he adds—By what justice and equity would we all bear the penalty of that sin, namely spiritual death, if that sin is not imputed to us?—first assumes what is in controversy between us, that original vice is inflicted on us by God and is a penalty properly so called. Next, the imputation of another's sin by which it becomes ours does not remove injustice but rather increases it: as if the most equitable and holy God first imputed another's sin to all men, to make them imputatively sinners and guilty, then to punish that imputed [sin] made them inherently sinners. So the Devil by his temptation would have made only one man a sinner; God by his act, that is imputation, would have made all men sinners and lost. How can it be that a pious conscience would not detest such a dogma? I find no further argument in this author that has not already been sufficiently refuted, so that there is no need to weary the Reader with empty repetition. Only this, which I had almost passed by, seems not to be dismissed without some censure—what he says in Thesis XLI: It is plain that whatever someone commits as head of some society or multitude is justly imputed to the whole community. For if that is true, the Romans were altogether badly dealt with when their head was Nero or Caligula: since whatever those wicked emperors committed could justly be imputed to each and every one of them; so there was no one in the whole Roman empire who was not a parricide, if parricide committed by the head was justly imputed to all Romans.

145: That learned man moves on to verse 19, and argues from it: we were made sinners by Adam's disobedience, therefore it was imputed to us. Through hereditary corruption—I grant; immediately—I deny. He seems bent on proving the consequence. Who, he asks, could that κατάστασις, that ἁμαρτία, that παράπτωμα make us guilty, or bring the παράπτωμα of Romans 5:18 (a judicial act, God's justice spoken out, and its effect: damnation, condemnation) upon us without actual sin, whether our own or imputed? Away with the delirium. The answer is plain. As Chamier puts it, it can make us guilty causally, by original sin produced and propagated into us. That is no delirium; it is the Church's settled doctrine, which Scripture and experience confirm. How, he adds, can we be constituted sinners in act without sin? Since that cannot be original sin—still only habitual, especially in the newly conceived or newborn—it must be some actual sin. I answer: we are constituted sinners not without sin, for original sin is truly sin. It is not an actual act; it is, in act, habitual sin: in act it inheres in infants; in act it makes us liable to God's wrath. Deny that, and you are scarcely off Pighius's path.
146: He also gibes at our reply—that the opposition's likeness lies in the thing, not in its mode—and says we take Socinus's part rather than Calvin's, when in fact he is the one leaving Calvin, to whom we hold fast. How does he refute the reply we already proved by authority and reason? He asks why our people then draw from this text the mode of justification, namely by imputing Christ's righteousness. A fine refutation! Who among ours draws that from here—Calvin, Martyr, Bucer, Bullinger, and the rest? Not at all; only later writers who leave their path on this point. They do not see, he says, how they wound the common cause when they let this supposedly invincible argument be torn from them—and, so far as they can, tear it from us to favor the other side. If we ask why they luxuriate so in this place, we shall find it is done to favor Pelagians, Arminians, Socinians, and Anabaptists. We see the opposite: they wound the common cause who cannot or will not argue well, push forward weak proofs as invincible, and meanwhile bury their brothers under slander. That we both see and lament.
147: I leave the rest—bare assertions without reason—and add only this, which both looks like an argument and shows how far our accusers leave our public Confession and drift toward Pighianism. If, he says, the first parent's sin is not imputed, why impute Christ's merits? Had he meant original sin or mediate imputation, he would not contradict our cause; he would only say something false and unfit for a theologian, let alone a Christian. We need Christ's righteousness imputed so we may also be justified from our many other sins. But when he means Adam's actual sin and its immediate imputation, who does not see that he denies original sin's guilt, and treats that sin as nothing for condemnation or justification? Sanctification that removes the disease is enough, he adds. Is it then a disease that is not sin, that does not condemn? Set that teaching beside Confession article XI: we believe this vice is truly sin, which makes every human being—even infants still in the womb—liable to eternal death before God. We also affirm that even after baptism it remains truly sin as to blame, though the sons of God are not therefore condemned, because God of free goodness and mercy does not impute it to them. We add that this perversity always bears some fruits of malice and rebellion.
148: You see this vice is truly sin, that it makes every man liable to eternal death before God unless it is forgiven—that it is imputed—and will you still deny we need Christ's merits imputed to be justified from it? So our opponents in this cause are guilty of the very charge they falsely lay on us: they leave the received doctrine. When he adds how excellent and wonderful our whole evangelical justification would look—yet from these φρονημάτα it must either fall wholly or at least become useless—you see, Reader, how false and slanderous that is. The same befell the distinguished D. Stephen Blancus, whose Theological Disputation on the soul's origin and how original sin is propagated appeared in 1648. In Thesis XLII he argues: all sinned by the sin that entered the world through one man; yet not in their own person, for they did not yet exist; therefore they sinned in Adam, for in him they died (1 Cor. 15:22). The conclusion could stand if rightly taken; but the minor looks like nothing but a denial of what article XI asserts in our Churches. He denies that the vice is the sin which entered the world—that is, all men—through one man; yet that article says the vice is truly sin and makes every human being liable to eternal death before God, which it could not do unless it had entered every human being.
149: His added words—'inasmuch as in him they died'—confirm our view. When all are said to die in Adam, we do not mean Adam's single death imputed to everyone, but death multiplied by the number of men, each his own. He adds that they died by that one man's offense (Rom. 5:15), and from this thinks it easy to gather that the offense was everyone's by imputation, since divine justice will not let someone share another's punishment without sharing the guilt somehow. If someone likewise said we were produced by that one man's power, would that power therefore be common to all by imputation? If justice forbids sharing another's punishment without sharing guilt, it also forbids making someone a sharer of guilt by the judge's imputation who otherwise would not share it. If a judge already acts unjustly in punishing one who shares no guilt, how much worse if by his own act and judicial imputation he also makes that man a guilty sinner who otherwise was neither? I marvel that pious and learned men miss this. Who that is innocent could not be 'justly' punished, if imputation makes common a sin that was not common, and makes a true sinner of one who otherwise was not?
150: At last the learned man says the Pauline word ἁμαρτίαν does not mean the habit of sin—the habitual corruption even in infants—but a past act of sinning, which can mean nothing but Adam's first sin. That contradicts Calvin and the other great men we follow, who take 'they sinned' of original vice. Still he offers reasons. I. Paul speaks of the sin that entered the world, that is all men, through Adam, called one man. So he assumes original vice is either not sin, or did not enter all naturally begotten through that one man. II. Infants too are wrapped in this sin: they count among those into whom death passed, and they die by no other actual sin than an imputed one, since no other actual sin befalls them; and that imputed actual sin is nothing but Adam's first. Yes, infants die by no other actual sin than Adam's first—but why not die proximately by that habitual vice which makes every human being liable to eternal death before God? As I have often said: you cannot build immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin without denying the guilt of habitual vice. III. When Paul says in verse 17 that death reigned through one offense, and in verse 19 that many were made sinners by one man's disobedience, those phrases can look only to Adam's own deed—the breach of God's command. Grant it—what then? Does it follow that ἁμαρτίαν does not mean the habit of sin, or that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately, before we are born corrupt? Death reigns through one offense so far as it is propagated by habit into all, so that death reigns in all because sin reigns. By one man's disobedience propagated and multiplied by habit, many are constituted sinners. Why hunt elsewhere for the proximate cause of our death, when that inhering sin shows itself in our body and members—and unless Christ's grace crucifies it, reigns so mightily in us?
151: In Thesis XLIII he adds that the death which passed to all through one man includes spiritual death—of the soul—nothing but the loss of original righteousness with the contrary habitual corruption set in its place. What is affirmed so easily can be denied as easily; it needed proof, which he does not even attempt. The Helvetic Confession and every better interpreter take that death of bodily and eternal death alone; that reading will be proved elsewhere. He adds that without imputing Adam's disobedience the derivation of habitual human corruption cannot be just. How can that be true? That derivation is nothing but sin's contagion and the spread of injustice; it is not itself just, nor can it be— for it is not just to multiply injustice. But God's permitting or not hindering that derivation is just and has nothing against justice. His further reason—by what justice would we all bear that sin's penalty, namely spiritual death, if it is not imputed?—first assumes what we dispute: that God inflicts original vice on us as a penalty properly so called. Next, making another's sin ours by imputation does not remove injustice but increases it: as if the most equitable and holy God first imputed another's sin to all, to make them sinners and guilty by imputation, then to punish that imputed sin made them sinners by inherence. So the Devil's temptation would have made only one man a sinner; God's act—imputation—would have made all men sinners and lost. How could a pious conscience not detest such a dogma? I find nothing more in this author not already refuted enough; empty repetition would only weary the Reader. One point I nearly passed: in Thesis XLI he says whatever someone commits as head of a society or multitude is justly imputed to the whole community. If that were true, the Romans were wholly wronged when Nero or Caligula was their head: whatever those wicked emperors did could justly be imputed to each Roman, so that no one in the empire was not a parricide if the head's parricide was justly charged to all.
